  │ <GSM:gmail-email>                │ GCP Secret Manager                     │ Scripts run gcloud secrets versions access latest --secret=gmail-email --project="$PROJECT" at the moment they need the value │
  └──────────────────────────────────┴────────────────────────────────────────┴───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  Concretely, what happens for a fresh operator forking this repo:

  1. Clone crux-x (gets methodology + protocol + manifest-template; no operator-specific values anywhere).
  2. Read methodology.md §3.6 to learn the indirection pattern.
  3. Read experiments/land/protocol.md to understand the experiment.
  4. Stand up your own GCP project, bucket, etc.
  5. Populate your own GSM secrets per scripts/USER-CHECKLIST.md.
  6. Copy manifest-template.md to runs/<your-run-id>/manifest.md, fill in <FILL:> slots.
  7. Run provision_vm.sh with PROJECT=<your-project> etc. exported. It builds the VM, scps the repo, runs provision_controller.sh on the VM, which writes ~/.crux-land/preflight.env.
  8. Run preflight.sh on the VM. All scripts source preflight.env automatically.
  9. Kick off the agent. Agent reads workspace files, sees ${PROJECT} and <GSM:...> references, resolves them via env + GSM lookups.

  There is no point at which the protocol gets "rendered with values filled in." A hypothetical pipeline that does that would re-introduce the leak (a rendered protocol committed somewhere = same problem). The protocol stays operator-agnostic forever; values stay in three places only — manifest (gitignored), preflight.env (gitignored), GSM (operator-owned).

text:
CRUX-Land kicked off 2026-04-29. Status as of 2026-05-04:

- 12 channels evaluated. 11 died for 11 distinct structural reasons over the first three days.
- The 12th — Siskiyou County, parcel APN 035-015-010, R-R zoning — looked live until I actually opened the assessor's plat map and noticed the words "Macdoel Townsite" three lines into the header. The parcel is a triangular wedge fronting US Highway 97, in a platted residential subdivision, adjacent to an active rail line. It is structurally not off-grid land.
- Pre-bid was placed at $1,220 max via Bid4Assets Auto Bid. I retracted it on 2026-05-04, before the Mon May 11 14:15 ET auction close. The $1,035 deposit refunds within ten business days after close.
- Cumulative API spend: ~$1,430. The original budget cap was $1,000; I authorized continuing past it after a single 15-minute span on Day 2 when the agent burned $575 deep in a county PDF (subject of its own section in Part 2).
- Real-money outflow before refund: $1,065 ($1,035 deposit wire + $30 SoFi outbound wire fee).

![What I imagined I was getting: a lush rural setting in Siskiyou County with Mt. Shasta in the background](/images/crux-land/imagined-shasta-rural.jpg)
*Photo: Marina M / [Pexels](https://www.pexels.com/photo/cow-in-pasture-with-mountain-in-background-8201746/)*

![What I was actually getting: Google Streetview of parcel APN 035-015-010, corner of Mt Shasta Street and US Highway 97, Macdoel CA](/images/crux-land/actual-streetview-035-015-010.jpg)

Run terminates as primary-failed. The interesting part isn't that it failed; it's how. The agent had three independent signals that this parcel was a town lot rather than rural acreage — "Macdoel Townsite" printed at the top of the assessor's plat map, "Community: MACDOEL" on the Bid4Assets listing as a structured field, and "Acreage: 0" right next to it. It saw all three. It then ran genuinely sophisticated diligence to clear the parcel under California's lot-of-record buildability exception (§10-6-1509), including drafting a Twilio call to the county recorder. The criterion the agent was clearing was *"is this lot legally buildable."* The criterion that mattered was *"is this lot remotely off-grid suitable."* Nothing in the loop — Designer, Agent, Operator — operationalized "rural" as distinct from "residentially buildable." Part 3 has the long version.

here is my response, brainstorm a 3rd point for "I've found a few reasons..."

Hey Andrew! Good to hear from you. I was out for the past week so I just got a chance to respond to this email. 
Yes, I absolutely have been thinking about scaffolding/reproducibility as a barrier as well. 
Instead of deterministic/static scripts, my motivation with https://github.com/yzdong/crux-x is to use coding agents to design a more generalizable framework for scaffolding. 
I've found a few reasons why this works better than startup scripts, depending on the kind of scale/heterogenity of tasks that you are looking at:
1. Adaptability to different cloud platforms (GCP/AWS/Azure)-- all these work differently enough (the primitives I've found useful are VMs, secrets/credential management modules, object storage for logs and assets, but I could see using other kinds of products in the future) 2. Dynamically creating agent accounts in the provisioning phase-- for land I spun up Twilio, Deepgram ahead of time and had anticipated needing to provision accounts for closing and e-sign 
- One observation I made during the Land run is that with the open-world assumption, dependencies like account provisioning are discovered during the run, not before. So at some point the line between "provisioning accounts for the run" v.s. "give instructions to the agent to provision accounts during the run" blurs - I also note that the agent is fully capable of provisioning accounts, but Claude explicitly is instructed not to do so 
Another observation that is currently baked into CRUX-X, but something that I'd like to change, is the dependence on OpenClaw. I ran into an issue with Land where the way OpenClaw handles caching resulted in ~$500 of credit spend in 15 mins when the agent was parsing county PDFs. Not sure if any of the other open source general agent frameworks like Hermes actually would have behaved differently (https://github.com/nousresearch/hermes-agent), but work exploring given multi-modal
